story_title: The House Where Night and Day Never Meet
place: The house of Night at the western edge of the world
summary: A lighthouse keeper tells of Nyx, goddess of Night, whose house at the world's edge never holds her and her daughter Day at once, and who sheltered Sleep from Zeus. Night walks the world each evening with Sleep in her arms.

teller.name: Ione
teller.who: keeper of a lighthouse on a far cape

listener: a night traveler resting on a stool in the warm lamp room of the lighthouse at dusk
hook: Which goddess was so old and respected that even Zeus held his temper rather than upset her?
context: Nyx is Night, one of the first beings born from Chaos; mother of Sleep, the Dreams and the Hesperides, and so old that Zeus himself stepped back from her door.
source_tradition: Ancient Greece (Hesiod's Theogony and Homer's Iliad)
source_note: Retold in original words from Hesiod and Homer (public domain); no modern translation or retelling was followed.

No faces, no text, no statues, no temples, no religious symbols.

script:
[[CHAPTER Welcome]]

Welcome to Fernwick Nights. Our story this evening is The House Where Night and Day Never Meet, a lesser-known tale from the Greek myths, told by Ione, who keeps a lighthouse on a far cape. Settle in wherever you are, and let the dark come slowly.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The One Zeus Would Not Upset]]

Take the stool by the window. The lamp room is the warmest place on the cape at this hour, and the brass is still holding the sun. I have a pot of tea steeping, with a spoonful of honey in it, and a tin of oat biscuits somewhere. Now, here is a question I have kept for you. Which goddess was so old and respected that even Zeus held his temper rather than upset her? Not Hera. Not Athena. Someone much quieter, and much older. Look out of the glass, and I think you will see her coming.

[pause]

First, let me tell you where you are. This is the lamp room, a round glass room at the very top of the tower, up ninety-two iron steps that ring when you climb them. The floor is cool boards, scrubbed pale. In the middle stands the great lens, a beehive of glass rings taller than I am, and when I lay my palm on it, it is faintly warm and humming. Behind me the kettle ticks as it cools on the little stove. There are woolen blankets folded on the chair. The wind outside makes a low, steady whistle round the rail, like someone idly blowing across a bottle, and under it comes the long slow drag of the waves on the rocks.

[pause]

Her name is Nyx. Night. In the oldest poems of Greece, she is not a small figure in the corner of the sky. She is one of the very first beings, born at the beginning of everything, out of the great yawning emptiness the Greeks called Chaos. Before the sea, before the mountains, before the sun had a road to travel, there was Night, and she was already old. The poet Hesiod, who gave us the family trees of the gods some twenty-seven centuries ago, calls her a goddess of great power.

[pause]

She had a husband of sorts, a being called Erebus, whose name means the deep shadow. Together they had two children, and I want you to notice what they were. Not more darkness. Light. Aether, the bright clear upper air, the blue where the gods live. And Hemera, Day. I have often thought it the loveliest joke in the oldest poems, that the first night made the first morning. Even in the beginning, the dark was carrying something bright inside it.

[pause]

She had a husband of sorts, a being called Erebus, whose name means the deep shadow. Together they had two children, and I want you to notice what they were. Not more darkness. Light. Aether, the bright clear upper air, the blue where the gods live. And Hemera, Day. I have often thought it the loveliest joke in the oldest poems, that the first night made the first morning. Even in the beginning, the dark was carrying something bright inside it.

[pause]

The sun is almost down now. The sea beyond the rocks has gone the color of a dark plum, and a single star has come out above the water, a clean white point, low in the west. The air through the open window smells of salt and cold stone, and a little of the lamp oil I trimmed an hour ago.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The House at the Edge of the World]]

Hesiod also describes where she lives. This is the part I like best. Far away, he says, at the western edge of the world, beyond the place where Atlas stands holding up the sky, there is a house. Its walls are wrapped in a dark cloud. Its doorway is a great threshold made of bronze, which no weather can wear, and its roots go down into the earth and cannot be moved.

[pause]

There, every evening, two sisters meet. Or nearly meet. Night is the elder, and her daughter is Day, whose name is Hemera. Each day, as the sun goes down, Night arrives at the bronze threshold from the east, and Day, coming home from her long walk over the land, reaches the same threshold from the west. They greet one another there. A few quiet words, perhaps. Then one steps in and the other steps out.

[long pause]

The old poet is very exact about this. The house, he says, is never big enough for both of them at once. When Night is inside, Day is out in the open, carrying her light over the earth. And when Day comes home, Night goes out, carrying in her arms the child she brought from the house: Sleep. That is how Hesiod puts it. Night walks over the world each evening with Sleep in her arms.

[pause]

I have always thought it a tender picture. A mother and daughter who share one house and never share a room. Each of them leaves the door ajar and the lamp lit for the other. And each of them gets a turn at the long road.

[long pause]

I think of them every evening when I light the lamp. I strike the match, and it flares with a sharp, sulfurous smell, and I touch it to the wick, and the flame takes hold, small and yellow, and then grows. The glass catches it and throws it out in a long white arm across the sea. It is a small thing to do, to light a lamp as the dark arrives. But I do it the way Day might leave a candle in the window for her mother, just inside the bronze door, so there is something warm to find.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER The Refuge]]

Now for Zeus, since I promised. In the Iliad, in book fourteen, Homer tells a small, funny story that shows how far Night's reach goes. Hera, Zeus's wife, wanted her husband out of the way for an afternoon, and so she went to Sleep, called Hypnos, and asked him to lull Zeus into a nap.

[pause]

Hypnos hesitated. He had done it once before, long ago, and Zeus had woken up in a towering temper. The king of the gods had searched the sky for the one who had put him to sleep, ready to throw him down into the sea. Sleep escaped by the narrowest margin. He ran to the only place he could think of, the house of Night, his mother. And she hid him.

[pause]

That was enough, Homer says. Zeus, furious as he was, stopped at her door. He did not want to do anything that might displease swift Night. Because even the lord of the thunder was careful with her. It is the only time in all the poems I know of when he simply turns around and goes home.

[long pause]

I find that charming. There is something very true in it. Anyone can be loud. It takes a different kind of power to be the one nobody wants to wake.

[long pause]

A fisherman's wife taught me that, years ago, when I first came to the cape. She walked up the tower stairs every night with a lantern and a loaf wrapped in cloth, because she was sure that keepers forget to eat. The bread was dark rye, still warm, with a crust that cracked when she tore it, and it smelled of caraway and smoke. She would sit where you are sitting and tell me the old stories, and mend a sock, and then go home down the ninety-two steps without a sound. I never heard her leave. She said that was the secret of the night: that nothing in it needs to announce itself.

[long pause]

[[CHAPTER Her Quiet Children]]

Hesiod gives Night a great many children, and I will tell you the gentler ones. There is Sleep, of course, and his brothers and sisters the Dreams, who go out each evening in their thousands, like leaves on a wind. There are the three Fates, who spin and measure the threads of life. And there are the Hesperides, the daughters of evening, who live in a garden of golden apples at the far edge of the world, and who sing as the light goes.

[pause]

It is a family of dusk. Not a loud one. I have a little notion that when the Greeks wanted to describe something that arrives on its own, with no one to ask it in, and leaves just as quietly, they gave it to Night to look after.

[pause]

The sun has gone. The lamp above us has begun to turn, slowly. A long soft finger of light sweeps the water, the rocks, and back. The tea has gone cool in the cup. Down below, a gull mutters once in its sleep, and the sea sighs against the foot of the cape. Gears click inside the pedestal, one tooth at a time, steady as a slow clock. Somewhere a rope taps a mast. The glass hums. The floor is warm under my slippers, and the blanket on the chair is soft and smells of wool and woodsmoke.

[long pause]

Night is out there now. She has left the threshold. Her daughter has gone in. She walks over the sea, and the hills, and the harbor, with her child in her arms. She does not hurry. She never has.

[long pause]

[[SECOND]]

[[CHAPTER Once More, Slowly]]

Which goddess did Zeus not wish to upset? The oldest one of all, Night.

[pause]

She lives in a house at the edge of the world, behind a threshold of bronze. Her daughter Day lives there too. They meet at the door, and one comes in, and one goes out.

[long pause]

Once, when Sleep was in trouble, he ran to her house. Zeus came after him, and stopped at her door, and went home.

[pause]

Each evening, Night walks over the world with Sleep in her arms. The lamp turns. The sea is slow. The star is out.

[long pause]

So that is the house where night and day never meet. The stool is yours, and the tea is warm enough, and the dark is very patient. Good night.
